whyItExists.problem: A program needs to do maths, compare values, and combine conditions. Without operators, you cannot calculate prices, validate input, or decide which code path to follow.
whyItExists.solution: JavaScript operators perform arithmetic, compare values, combine logical conditions, and assign results. They are the fundamental building blocks of all computation.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Constantly — in every expression that calculates, compares, or combines values.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid the loose equality operators == and !=. Use === and !== instead.

explainModes.beginner: Operators are maths symbols and comparison signs. + adds numbers, - subtracts, * multiplies. === checks if two values are equal. && means 'and', || means 'or'.
explainModes.simple: JavaScript has arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %, **), assignment (=, +=, -=), comparison (===, !==, >, <, >=, <=), logical (&&, ||, !), and a few special ones (?, ??, typeof).
explainModes.standard: Operator precedence determines evaluation order (PEMDAS applies). Short-circuit evaluation means && stops at the first falsy value and || stops at the first truthy one. The nullish coalescing operator (??) returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined — unlike || which triggers on any falsy value.
explainModes.technical: The optional chaining operator (?.) safely accesses nested properties — obj?.a?.b returns undefined instead of throwing if any level is null/undefined. The logical assignment operators (&&=, ||=, ??=) combine logical checks with assignment. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) operate on 32-bit integers and are rarely needed in application code.
explainModes.deepDive: JavaScript's + operator is overloaded: for numbers it adds, for strings it concatenates, and for mixed types it coerces to string. This is the source of '5' + 3 = '53'. The abstract equality algorithm (==) has complex rules with 20+ type-coercion cases. The strict equality algorithm (===) is simple: same type and same value. Always use strict.

content.code:
10 + 3   // 13  — addition
10 - 3   // 7   — subtraction
10 * 3   // 30  — multiplication
10 / 3   // 3.333...  — division
10 % 3   // 1   — remainder (modulo)
10 ** 2  // 100 — exponentiation (10 squared)

// Assignment shorthand
let x = 10;
x += 5;   // x = 15  (same as x = x + 5)
x -= 3;   // x = 12
x *= 2;   // x = 24
x /= 4;   // x = 6
x++;      // x = 7  (increment by 1)
x--;      // x = 6  (decrement by 1)

// Always use strict equality
5 === 5      // true  — strict equal (same type AND value)
5 !== 3      // true  — strict not equal
5 > 3        // true  — greater than
5 < 3        // false — less than
5 >= 5       // true  — greater than or equal
5 <= 4       // false — less than or equal

// Loose equality — AVOID
5 == '5'     // true  — converts types
0 == false   // true  — confusing
null == undefined  // true  — very confusing

// String comparison (lexicographic)
'apple' < 'banana'  // true — alphabetical order
'Z' < 'a'           // true — uppercase letters sort before lowercase

questions.question: What does the % operator do?
questions.explanation: % is the modulo (remainder) operator. 10 % 3 = 1 because 10 ÷ 3 = 3 remainder 1. It is commonly used to check if a number is even (n % 2 === 0).

questions.question: What is the difference between || and ??
options: || falls back on any falsy value; ?? only falls back on null or undefined
?? falls back on any falsy value; || only falls back on null or undefined
|| is for strings, ?? is for numbers
questions.explanation: || returns the right side for any falsy value (0, '', false, null, undefined). ?? returns the right side ONLY for null or undefined. Use ?? when 0 or empty string are valid values you want to keep.

faq.a: NaN stands for 'Not a Number'. It is the result of invalid numeric operations like 0/0 or parseInt('hello'). Confusingly, typeof NaN === 'number'. Use Number.isNaN(value) to check for it.

faq.q: What is the difference between ++ before and after a variable?
faq.a: x++ (post-increment) returns the current value THEN increments. ++x (pre-increment) increments first THEN returns the new value. In most cases this distinction doesn't matter — the end result (x is incremented) is the same.

examples: E-commerce sites use % to apply 'every 3rd item free' discounts
Authentication checks use && to ensure a user is both logged in AND verified
Config values use ?? to provide defaults without overriding valid falsy values like 0
